inline.s: The transmission of Elder Zhuan records that in that year snow fell in heavy flurries for ten full days, and the snow of every terrace summit was swept into one pile, burying the hermitage of the Dragon Gate to a depth of more than a hundred feet. The Master and Master Che shut their doors and sat motionless, stirring up the fire but once a day to warm their tea and rice. The congregations of North Terrace, White Horse Temple, and Central Terrace, two or three hundred souls in all, devoted themselves to taking up hoes, mattocks, baskets, and brooms, and lowered probing poles down the terrace heights to seek the road to the Dragon Gate. They probed and dug as they came, going and returning; the congregation labored so bravely that only after two full days of probing did they at last reach the hermitage. They shouted for joy, entered the door, and all declared: 'That after such a calamity amid these mountains a fire should still stand — this is the protection of the Buddhas and of Heaven.' The Master and Master Che gave thanks, then said: 'Yet one must pass through it before one gains it.' Thereupon they melted snow into a warm broth and joyfully served the whole congregation. The next day the mountain monasteries, hearing that the two masters were safe, came bearing rice, flour, fruit, and sweetmeats until there was scarcely room to set a foot. Later it was also heard that, dwelling once together with Master Miao, he too had met this great snow and dissolved it by entering samādhi. Snow and ice of the Dragon Gate came to be regarded as nothing out of the ordinary, and so the chronicle for the most part does not record them.
The fifth year, dīngchǒu ●

At thirty-two years of age, in spring, I returned from Yanmen. Because I reflected that I could never repay the boundless kindness of my parents, and also because I felt myself beset by many obstacles in the Dharma, I read the Vow Text of Master Si of Nanyue and resolved to pierce my tongue, to mix my blood with gold-dust, and to write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sūtra — above, to bind the excellent karmic conditions with prajñā; below, to repay the boundless kindness of my parents — and in this year the project first sprang up. Earlier, the Compassionate Sage Mother, for the protection of the state, had chosen monks to chant sūtras, and I had presumptuously been set down among them. When now the emperor learned of the sūtra-copying, he straightway bestowed gold and paper to assist it. In the fourth month of the next year the copying was begun. At that time Master Chekong returned to Mount Kuang, and I composed ten poems to see him off. (The Compassionate Sage Mother is the Empress Dowager Li — a first appearance. Master Chekong — a second appearance.)

[Piercing the tongue and writing the Avatamsaka Sūtra in blood and gold] Piercing the tongue to draw blood, and blending it with gold-dust, to write out one Avatamsaka Sūtra. Master Yinguang says: 'When Master Hanshan copied the sūtra, it was the Empress Dowager who supplied the paper and the gold. The paper for gold writing must be blue for it to show; on white paper it does not show.
...as when Hanshan, at the Miaode Nunnery on Wutai, pierced his tongue, ground gold with his blood, and wrote out the Avatamsaka Sūtra.' (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter in Reply to Master Hongyi, No. 1)

Zheng's note: That he wrote the Avatamsaka in blood is precisely what later is spoken of when, sharing Master Miao's vow, he established the unhindered assembly and placed the sūtra in the pagoda treasury. The vow had not yet been written when a spiritual response was already felt. The 'the emperor heard and bestowed gold and paper' refers to the fact that, because his name had been placed on the roster of sūtra-chanters, the Sage Mother heard of it and bestowed it — it does not mean the Wanli emperor. The bestowing of the writing gold and paper for the Bao'en Temple, and this matter, are the beginning of the Sage Mother's karmic conditions emerging into the world.

The Compassionate Sage, Empress Dowager Li, was the Wanli emperor's legal mother. She believed in the Buddha with great ardor and gave alms with great fullness, and the people of the capital called her the Old Lady of the Buddha and the Taoists.
The sixth year, wùyín ●

At thirty-three years of age, I bent my whole mind to copying the sūtra; whether the stroke was large or small, with each falling brush I uttered a recitation of the Buddha's name. Whatever monks or laymen from the roaming mountains came, I always had the attendant announce them. Though my hand never ceased from the writing, yet I did not fail in responding to them; whoever came to ask after me I would exchange a few words with. The eminent and my old friends I would invite to take a seat on the meditation couch, converse face to face without missing anything, and still without hindering the writing; when they compared against the master copy on the table, not one stroke was misplaced. Each day I was as always, without the slightest trace of agitation. The old masters of the neighboring districts, secretly thinking it strange, one day led a crowd to test me, deliberately making a disturbance; and when the writing was done and read through, they truly believed. They asked Master Miao, 'How can Master Yin be capable of this?' Master Miao said, 'My friend has but entered this samādhi until it is thoroughly ripe.' Since I took to the mountains, up to the copying of the sūtra, I repeatedly had auspicious dreams. On the first night I dreamed I entered the Vajra Grotto, with the Great Prajñā Monastery beside the stone gate; when I went in I found it vast as empty space, its halls and towers solemn and lovely beyond compare. In the main hall there was only a great couch, and I saw Master Qingliang [Chengguan] leaning reclined upon it, with Master Miao standing in attendance on the left. I hurried to bow, took my place on the right, and heard the Master give instruction: first he set forth the vision of the perfect and interpenetrating realm of the dharmadhātu — that Buddha-lands enter into one another, that lord and retinue intermingle, in the motion of coming and going without movement. Even as he spoke, that realm appeared before my eyes. I knew of myself that body and mind were interpenetrating and at ease. When the instruction ended, Master Miao asked, 'What realm is this?' The Master smiled and said, 'A realm of no realm.' When I awoke, I saw that mind and realm had fused together, with no further doubt or obstruction. On another night I dreamed that I trod in the void and ascended, higher and higher, with no limit above; then I fell, and saw that the ten directions were utterly devoid of anything — only the ground was level as a mirror, clear as lapis lazuli. Looking far off I saw only a vast tower, no smaller than the sky. Within it were gathered all the people and affairs of the world — down to the meanest traffic of the market-streets — all contained within it, and none going beyond. In the tower a high seat was set, of a purple-gold flame-color, and to my mind it was the adamant jewel throne. The tower was so solemn and exquisite as to be beyond thought. I was overjoyed and wished to draw near, but thought within myself, 'How, within the realm of purity and coolness, can there be this defilement?' The instant this thought arose, the tower grew distant. Then I thought again, 'Purity and defilement are but born of my own mind,' and the tower drew near. Presently I saw, arrayed before the seat, a congregation of monks, tallest of body and most dignified beyond compare. Suddenly a monk came forth from behind the seat, holding an opened scroll of sūtra, and handed it me, saying, 'The Master has just declared this sūtra and specially sends word to bestow it on you.' I received it, unrolled it, and saw it was written in gold in Sanskrit characters, which I could not read, so I tucked it away; then I asked who the Master was. He said, 'Maitreya.' I rejoiced, and followed the monk upward until I reached the stair of the tower, where I closed my eyes, gathered my thoughts, and stood. Suddenly I heard the sound of a chime; I opened my eyes and saw that Maitreya had already taken his seat. I straightway gazed in reverence, and looking up beheld his face, dazzling with purple-gold radiance, such as nothing in the world could match. When the bowing was done, I thought, 'Now he has spoken for my sake, so I am the one addressed.' Then I knelt long, unrolled the scroll, and heard him say: 'Discrimination is consciousness-knowledge; non-discrimination is prajñā. Through consciousness one is defiled; through prajñā one is pure. In defilement there is birth and death; in purity there is no Buddha.' At that point body and mind suddenly became void; I only heard within the sky a sound, distinctly and clearly — and when I awoke, the words seemed still ringing in my ears. From this, the distinction between consciousness and prajñā was clear in my heart and eyes, and I knew that where I had been was the Tuṣita heaven, the tower of Maitreya Buddha. On yet another night I dreamed a monk came to tell me that on the summit of North Terrace Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was preparing a bath and inviting me. I went with him and entered a vast, pure, and bright hall, filled with fragrance. The attendants were all Indian monks; they led me to the bath-house, where I undressed and entered the pool, and saw that one person was already in it. On looking, it was a woman. My mind revolted and I would not enter, but the one in the pool deliberately expanded her form, showing her to be a man. Then I went in and bathed with him. He scooped water in his hand to wash me, pouring it over me from the head down into my very viscera, as if scraping out a tub of flesh; the five organs were washed clean one by one, leaving only a skin like a cage of lapis lazuli, wholly translucent. Then the one in the pool called for tea, and I saw an Indian monk holding half a skull, split like a melon; looking at it, the marrow was dripping wet, and my mind revolted at it. The monk then picked this out with his finger and showed it me, saying, 'Is this not unclean?' and put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus he scooped and ate; it was sweet as honey. When the brain was all eaten there remained only blood and water, and the one in the pool said, 'Give it to him.' The monk then handed it to me, and I took it and drank, and its taste was like sweet dew. I drank it down, and it went through the pores of my whole body, trickling out from every one. When the drinking was done the Indian monk rubbed my back, and with a great slap of his palm I woke. My whole body was drenched in sweat like water, and my viscera were wholly transparent. From then on body and mind were as if washed clean, in a lightness beyond words. Dreams such as these were more often auspicious than not. In sum, they were all my communing with the saints — and once, hearing the Buddha's words that one in such a state has many good dreams, I believed it. (Master Miaofeng — a fifth appearance.)

Zheng, serving by his side in attendance, had often seen the works of the Hanshan Master's calligraphy, both regular and running, of twin excellence, all grounded in the standards of the two Wangs, passing in and out with transformation. While copying the Avatamsaka in blood, he did not stop his brush, and did not refuse visitors; every stroke he wrote was accompanied by a recitation of the Buddha's name; though a worthy sat in converse, still the writing did not stop. Comparing against the master copy on the table, not one character was misplaced. Without a great samādhi and great spiritual power, how could there be not the slightest misplacement? If I lay out the great dream-samādhi he tells: in one dream he saw Master Qingliang face to face, in the Vajra Grotto, leaning on the couch to bestow the prophecy, and straightway the realm came present before him, body and mind without obstruction. In each of these he never once forgot Qingliang, never forgot the karmic bond with Master Miao. Again he dreamed of going to the Tuṣita heaven, to Maitreya's tower, where he saw in person the solemn jewel throne, and Maitreya Buddha commanded a monk to bestow the sūtra; on mounting the seat he saw before him and heard the teaching on defilement and purity, clear in his ears, and so gained the distinction of consciousness and prajñā, transparent in heart and eye. A third dream took him in person to the bath that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva prepared on the summit of North Terrace — a foul woman, expanding to man — which is but the Hanshan Master's youth-body manifesting, one mind unconfused, originally pure, with not the slightest taint, so that he could enter the sea of fragrant water and shed his skin and change his bone. Again there appeared in strange mutation the good and the foul, the pure and the defiled, the startled loathing and the clinging love — all manner of forms wholly transformed, and all five colors without a master. In the end it was like Fotucheng, who before the water split open his breast and thoroughly washed his stomach and intestines, his body translucent as lapis lazuli. In the end it was like Huangbo and Linji, one blow leaving a mark, one slap drawing blood. In the end it was like Confucius who saw in person King Wen and Duke Zhou, in length and shortness, black and white. With the eyes shut or open, there is nothing that is not a true dream. Clear in his own person, his will and spirit like spirit — the true is the dream-true, the dream is the true-dream; therefore it is said the perfect man has no dreams. Even so, had he not abandoned body and life, sinking deep into that pile of snow and ice, buried alive for six years, and died the great death several times over — how could he come alive out of death, thrust his head from the great dream, wrap heaven and earth, blaze through ancient and modern, and become a measureless great man? And if he had not, today in this body of flesh, sitting upright, manifesting at Caoxi, sealing Qingliang in the north and serving Master Lü in the south, from the head of Dayu ridge where the robe and bowl were seized, dying and living again, three turns and nine bends, renewing two temples — then in the Hanshan Dharma-cloud, on the tip of a single hair was raised the jewel-king's realm; and on the day he took up pen and paper to narrate his own chronicle, he would have been no more than a single hard-working old man of the world, turning his heart to the honored elders. The Chan monks of all quarters, who saw the record of the three dreams during his lifetime, must surely laugh at it as idle talk; those who heard of the three dreams after his death will even revile it as a realm of demons. Only the Hanshan Master himself had confidence to the full; and in all the world, now and hereafter, there is not one who can attain equal confidence. Now I know that Maitreya's bestowal of the scroll wholly certifies the coming age to be as the beginningless age; and that Mañjuśrī's bath was to bathe the body of skin and flesh into the body of the adamantine stage. As Zheng marshals his commentary to this point, in a daze he dreams his way into Caoxi; and within the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the inconceivable, he folds his palms and says: 'Rare is the World-Honored One.'
The seventh year, jǐmǎo ●

At thirty-four years of age: in autumn of that year, the building of the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple in the capital was completed. Originally the Sage Mother, to offer the merits to the late emperor and to protect the holy person of the sovereign, wished to rebuild the Sarira Jewel Pagoda at Taya Temple on Wutai. She commanded the ministers, but because the mountain was so far from the capital, they chose an auspicious site near the city and built the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple there. When the works were done and the report returned, the Sage Mother felt that the Wutai vow was still unfulfilled, so she commanded the emperor still to send eunuchs, with three thousand workmen, to the mountain to build. At this time the court had just begun its Buddhist works, and the eunuchs were sent out for the first time; I feared the works could not be completed, and that the Dharma-gate would suffer. At that time I did all in my power to mediate between them, so that from first to last all went well. (The Sage Mother — a third appearance. The late emperor, Longqing — a first appearance. The emperor, Wanli — a first appearance.)

Zheng once, following the crowd, went to the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple built by the Compassionate Sage, Empress Dowager Li, arriving by way of the Tongzhou water route to Zhangjiawan, and entered the temple. It is fifteen li south of Tongzhou city and twenty-five li north to the Haidai Gate of the capital. The locals say the place had long been a ruined shrine, popularly called the Horse House Temple; the Old Lady of the Buddha and the Taoists, on its old site, renewed it in grand style and conferred on it the title of Great Compassionate Longevity. In front they invited the Hanshan Master, and behind they invited Master Daguan, and both dwelt in this temple. The chronicle records in large letters that in the autumn of this year the capital's Great Compassionate Longevity Temple was completed — thus we see that the karmic conditions of his entering the capital to spread the Dharma and bring calamity upon himself began here. Truly one who has attained the Dharma holds a life hanging by a thread; for first he had risen up in righteousness — such is the style of the Spring and Autumn annals.
The eighth year, gēngchén ●

At thirty-five years of age: in that year a special edict ordered a survey of lands and grain throughout the empire, not sparing a single inch. Wutai had never been entered in the register, but a villain of the county, to deceive and conceal, wished to transfer a levy of five hundred measures of grain onto Wutai, repeatedly sending documents to inspect and report the land; and throughout all the mountains' monasteries and hermitages, there was not a single person who could be at ease — from this the mountain became a fox's den. The elders of the mountains told me of it, and I said, 'Be at peace; let the masters have no worry, and I will slowly manage it.' So I bent my effort and found ways and means, laying the matter before the authorities, and in the end won exemption from the survey, without adding so much as a measure. The Wutai sanctuary was thereby preserved entire.
Zheng knows that conditioned meritorious deeds, if regarded as unconditioned meritorious deeds, are naturally accomplished.
The ninth year, xīnsì ●

At thirty-six years of age, I established the unhindered assembly. At first Master Miao had also pierced his blood and written the Avatamsaka Sūtra, sharing with me the vow to build a perfect sanctuary, called the unhindered assembly. Master Miao begged alms, and money and grain were gathered; from the capital were invited of great virtuous and famous monks five hundred. All the arrangements for the sanctuary were complete, when it happened that the emperor issued an edict praying for an heir, sending officials to Wudang; and the Sage Mother sent officials to Wutai, to the very temple. I thought that all the Buddhist rites performed by monks are but to pray for the state and secretly assist the imperial destiny. Now that the prayer for an heir was the very root of the state, nothing was greater. I wished to merge all the work prepared for the sanctuary into the single matter of praying for an heir, and not to do it for the sake of my own little reputation. Master Miao could not understand; and the envoy sent by the emperor also did not understand the matter, but only sought to curry favor. I strongly disagreed and contended against them, opposing them, yet in the end my counsel was followed. But the reputation of opposing the eunuch envoy also got abroad. Presently, when the southern seditious men stirred up trouble in Jiangnan, those who envied me wished to use it to wound me and break up the sanctuary. Yet because the matter was billed as praying for an heir for the state, it was preserved unharmed from first to last. That year the pagoda was completed, and I straightway placed the gold-written Avatamsaka Sūtra in its treasury, with a single scroll of vow-text. I myself begged alms to make the Avatamsaka world revolving-treasure-reel, to be used on setting up the sanctuary; and all the offerings, vessels, utensils, and provisions — everything needed. Master Miao, in the capital, seemed not to know of it; all was managed by me alone, for ninety days and ninety nights without closing my eyes. When the tenth month came, Master Miao led the more than five hundred monks he had invited, all assembled in a single day, a thousand or more within and without; and their lodging, offerings, tea and rice were all in order, without confusion, and no one knew whence it came — the onlookers were all astonished. At the very start was opened a water-land ceremony of seven days and nights; and during those seven days I ate not a single grain, only drinking water. Yet I did not fail in any duty, offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, changing five hundred tables of offerings each day, all in due order without loss, and no one knew whence they came. The onlookers thought it a divine operation; I myself knew it was the aid of the Buddhas' power. (The Sage Mother — a third appearance; the emperor — a second appearance; the heir apparent, Taichang — a first appearance; Master Miaofeng — a sixth appearance.)

Zheng was born in the Shenzong reign and knows that the matter of contending for the heir apparent was the greatest. What the Hanshan Master's appearance in the world most concerned was that the heir-apparent matter came first: his merit lay in being the first to advocate it, and in the princes who settled the succession, in order to plan for the spirit of the state, and not in attaching themselves to the later debates over the succession as a means to open the gate of factional calamity. The blood-written sūtra, the unhindered assembly, are the first cause of the prayer for an heir. The emperor sent eunuchs to Wudang, secretly to pray for an heir for Consort Zheng — and the prayer was to the Taoists. The Sage Mother sent eunuchs to Wutai, secretly to pray for an heir for the Consort Wang — and the prayer was to the monks. Each had their own faith and their own petition. The eunuch, spying the emperor's intent and fearing the unpredictable, therefore set his heart on currying favor, and grew of two minds toward the Sage Mother's command, unwilling to merge the blood-completed and unhindered sanctuary that he and Master Miao had made with the prayer for an heir, so as to display a great feat. For the unhindered assembly had been gathered by alms, and had no bearing on the prayer for an heir; and the prayer for an heir was sent within, apart from the unhindered assembly. Thus Master Miao could not understand, so he was looking at the Buddhist level; the Hanshan Master contended with all his strength, fixing his heart on the foundation of the state. The excellent karmic conditions happened to gather, and his single-minded sincerity reached Heaven. Managing alone, he went ninety days and nights without closing his eyes. The whole company of monks assembled, and for seven days he drank water and ate no grain. The minutest tasks were done as by ghosts, and the great offerings operated as by spirits. Without the radiance of samādhi, how could he have drawn the aid of the Buddhas' power so abundantly? Afterwards, when the calamity arose at Mt. Lao, the emperor's words said, 'All the court is for the monks; I alone am for the Taoists' — this distantly binds up the Wudang-Wutai case.
The tenth year, rénwǔ ●

At thirty-seven years of age: in the spring of that year I expounded the Xuántán of the Avatamsaka; for a hundred days the resident monks and the gathered laity from all quarters, day by day not fewer than ten thousand people, ate at one meal as if sitting in a single hall, without mixing or confusion, without a sound of a herald or a knock at the door. All was disposed by me alone, with no one else to give orders, and the wise could not tell how it was done. So of my whole life's energy, here it was nearly exhausted. When the assembly ended I examined what remained in the storehouse — all manner of money and grain, some ten thousand and more — and sealed and consigned it all to the abbot of the temple, to be the enduring property. Then Master Miao and I, with a single bowl, went off light and free. Master Miao went to Luya; I, being ill, went to the Zhangshi Cliff at Zhending to recuperate. I composed a poem containing the lines, 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun / On the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.' In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born, and I went again to the Zhongfeng Temple west of the capital, writing a preface to the re-engraved Zhongfeng Collected Records, and passed the winter in a water-fasting at a stone chamber. (Master Miaofeng — a seventh appearance; the crown prince, Taichang — a second appearance.)

Zheng reckons: in the tenth month of xīnsì, because of praying for the imperial heir, the great unhindered sanctuary was built at the Great Pagoda Temple on Wutai, completing the merits of seven days and nights; and fittingly, in the eighth month of the following year, rénwǔ, the palace concubine Consort Wang bore the heir Taichang. The chronicle writes in large letters: 'In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born.' Before the heir was yet born, he already wrote of the heir; when the heir had not yet been fixed as crown prince, he wrote straight out 'crown prince' — great indeed is the style of the Spring and Autumn annals! Reckoning the ten months of a human gestation, the immaculate certainty of it plainly shows that this was the Buddha's and the patriarchs' miraculous incarnation and birth. Thus the great treasure was at last mounted, and his benevolence was suddenly spread; though the state's fortune was near its end and the reign changed, it did not perish — and this was well so. Consort Wang, after the succession was fixed, was made Noble Consort Gong, and died in the thirty-seventh year. When Guangzong ascended the throne, she was posthumously titled Empress Xiaojing. At her death it was kept secret and not reported abroad, and only after four days, at the petition of the ministers, was it announced. At that time the envoy Shen Youze submitted a memorial asking for increased rites, but it was not answered. The affairs of the inner palace are hard to speak of. From this, Master Miao parted from the Hanshan Master; two years later they went together to the capital to receive the imperial bounty, and it seems they never saw each other again. The Hanshan Master, having completed eight years passing in and out of Wutai, now went off: a great cultivation, a great realization, a great sanctuary, a great working of his powers, a great spiritual response, sealing up a handful of treasury and ten-thousand-some of money and grain, and with a single bowl went lightly off. Before this, the Dragon Gate of Wutai made a great conclusion, a great scattering, 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun / On the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.' After this, Mt. Lao and Caoxi made a great prophecy, a great transformation. The clear-eyed can themselves grasp it.
Here ends the matter of the ascetic practice and Tao-completion at Wutai.
The eleventh year, guīwèi ●

At thirty-eight years of age, in the first month of spring, the water-fast was finished. Yet because of the empty reputation of Wutai — thinking that under a great name it is hard to dwell long — I took to the Eastern Sea, and here first changed my name to Hanshan; from this moment I no longer knew myself as Chengyin. At first, when the temple was burned down, my resolve was to restore it; so I did the ascetic practice while awaiting the conditions. But having dwelt eight years at Wutai with some opportunities, I feared that to wait longer would lose the time, and so I hid at the Eastern Sea — this was my true resolve. On the eighth day of the fourth month of summer I reached Mt. Lao. When Master Miao first parted from me, thinking I could not go alone, he assigned the Dharma-companion Dezong to be my attendant, and he followed me. I had earlier read the Avatamsaka Commentary, in the chapter on the abodes of the Bodhisattvas, which says, 'In the Eastern Sea there is a place called the Nārayaṇa Grotto, where since of old the hosts of Bodhisattvas have dwelt.' The Qingliang Commentary says, 'In Sanskrit, nārayaṇa means enduring and firm — this is the Mt. Lao of the Eastern Sea.' In the Tribute of Yu, this is the Dengzhou-Laizhou region, and the grotto exists to this day. Because I admired it, I made a special visit, and on reaching Mt. Lao indeed found the place; but it was not livable. I then explored the deepest recess of the mountain's south side, backing upon a multitude of peaks and facing the swallowing sea, utterly exquisite and strange, truly not a place of the human world. The place was called the Avalokiteshvara Hermitage — an old shrine, but only its ruined foundations remained. On investigation, in the early Yuan, the Seven Perfect Ones had come forth in the East and, borrowing the prestige of Shizu, seized many Buddhist temples and turned them into Taoist abbacies. When Shizu returned from his western campaigns and the monks pleaded, many were ordered restored. Only Mt. Lao, hidden on the sea, had not been reached, and so all was in ruins. I delighted in its seclusion — a place truly to flee humankind and quit the world — and resolved to dwell there. At first I spread a single mat under a tree; after seven months, I won the layman Zhang Daxin, a man of the district, to cut brush and raise a hut for me to live in. A full year passed with no one coming or going, and my heart was greatly at ease. At that time the Guifeng Dharma-master of the Ling Mountain Temple in Jimo — a very eye of the region — was delighted to be acquainted. (Dezong, the Dharma-companion of Master Miao; the layman Zhang Daxin; and the Dharma-master Guifeng — a first appearance for each.)
